newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian MTBE-September trades at year high of $280/T.
newsitem.headline: Asian MTBE-September trades at year high of $280/T.

text.p: Asian MTBE prices on Wednesday have hit $280 per tonne, the highest level in the year, and have room to move higher, industry sources said.
"Even a year ago it was not at $280," said an Asian producer. "Prices have been very weak but stable in the past year."
Singapore free-on-board (fob) prices have been on the rise since June, mainly on the back of strong U.S prices.
U.S. MTBE values have been on a bull run in the past month, supporting both NYMEX crude and gasoline levels earlier this week.
With Singapore August supplies already sold out, producers were offering and trading September parcels as high as $280 fob. A week ago, sellers were at $10 lower.
And sellers still expected a further hike as Singapore prices are lagging by $60 per tonne below the U.S. West Coast.
"There are signs that we will see the gap close further...at least by another $15-$20," a Mideast producer said. "Both good demand and tight supplies are the factors."

Traders said Asian blending demand was good amid tight supplies of high octane gasoline as output from reformers have been cut due to high feedstock costs. Malaysia and the Philippines also emerged with high-octane gasoline requirements.
Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) is seeking both its September requirements of MTBE and reformate with a 2.0-percent MTBE content.
Both tenders closed on July 29 and traders expect awards later on Wednesday at much firmer levels than the last awards.
CPC's August purchases of two cargoes of 3,500 tonnes of MTBE were at $270 per tonne cost-and-freight (c-and-f) while it bought its reformate at $23.30 per barrel, c-and-f, traders said.

Last week, Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC) was awarded Thailand's Bangchak Petroleum Plc's import tender for August MTBE at a much higher price at around $275 per tonne c-and-f, compared to its July award at $263, c-and-f.
"The current Asian demand is very good, but the catalyst is the U.S. West Coast. Asian buyers have to compete with U.S. buyers's levels," a producer said.

Supplies in this region are also tight as Mideast producers prefer to move cargoes to the U.S. rather than to Asia and as the bulk of Asia's supplies in August and September have been or are expected to be sold to the U.S. West Coast, sources said.

The MTBE rise in the U.S. is due to tight supplies caused by periodic production problems earlier this year. But inventories are likely to improve in the second half of August due to the restart of imports and improvements in U.S. Gulf productions, traders said.
Traders in Asia, however, did not expect Singapore prices to tumble.
"Maybe in September it will come down a bit because it (the U.S.) will be out of the blending season, but it will be a gradual fall, not a big one," the seller said.
